headline: The biggest adjustment is Korea's strict seniority-based formality — honorifics, two-handed exchanges, and drinking rituals — which goes well beyond the polite deference you're used to at home.

watch_outs.title: Pour and receive drinks two-handed
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines everyone pours their own glass and toasts casually with 'tagay' among peers.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Korea you never pour your own drink; the youngest pours for elders, glasses are held with both hands, and you turn your head away when drinking in front of a senior.
watch_outs.do: Let others fill your glass and refill theirs first, holding the bottle with both hands and turning slightly aside when you drink before an elder.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not pour your own soju or clink glasses while looking a senior straight in the eye as you drink.

watch_outs.title: Use honorifics and titles with elders
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines you can address seniors by first name or 'Kuya/Ate' and switch easily between formal and casual English.
watch_outs.to_norm: Korean speech levels (jondaetmal) and titles like 'sajangnim' or 'seonsaengnim' are expected with anyone older or senior, and casual speech can offend.
watch_outs.do: Learn a few honorific greetings and use titles plus the person's surname until invited to speak more casually.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not address an older colleague or your host's parents by first name or drop into casual speech.

watch_outs.title: Two hands for cards and gifts
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines business cards are handed over casually with one hand and often pocketed without reading.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Korea cards and gifts are given and received with both hands, and the card is read carefully before being put away respectfully.
watch_outs.do: Offer and receive business cards and gifts with both hands, then read the card and place it on the table rather than in your pocket.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not hand over a business card one-handed or stuff it straight into your wallet.

watch_outs.title: No tipping at restaurants
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines you check for a service charge and otherwise leave about 10% in cash with the server.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Korea the menu price is the final price; staff may chase you to return cash left on the table.
watch_outs.do: Pay exactly the bill and say 'gamsahamnida' as thanks instead of leaving extra money.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not leave a tip on the table at an ordinary Korean restaurant or cafe.

watch_outs.title: Chopsticks never upright in rice
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines you eat with fork and spoon and rest utensils however is convenient.
watch_outs.to_norm: Standing chopsticks upright in rice evokes funeral and ancestral rites and makes Koreans at the table uncomfortable.
watch_outs.do: Lay chopsticks flat on the table or a rest between bites.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not stick your chopsticks vertically into a bowl of rice.

watch_outs.title: Slurping noodles is welcome
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines you eat mami or batchoy quietly with a spoon and slurping is a minor faux pas.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Korea loud slurping of noodles shows appreciation and is normal at the table.
watch_outs.do: Slurp your noodles freely and enjoy the sound as a compliment to the cook.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not apologize for or suppress slurping sounds at a Korean noodle restaurant.

watch_outs.title: Beckon with palm down, not finger
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines curling one finger upward to call someone is seen as demeaning, so you use a palm-down scratching wave.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Korea the palm-down wave is also the polite way to call someone, especially someone younger or a server.
watch_outs.do: Call people over with your palm facing down and fingers waving toward you.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not curl a single index finger upward to beckon anyone.

watch_outs.title: Bow instead of cheek kisses
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines you greet friends and family with a light cheek-to-cheek touch and a 'mwah' sound.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Korea greetings with elders and new acquaintances are a bow, often with both hands, and physical contact is minimal.
watch_outs.do: Bow slightly to your host's parents and elders, and offer a handshake only if they extend one.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not lean in for a cheek kiss or a hug when meeting Korean elders for the first time.

watch_outs.title: Punctuality matters in business
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines relaxed 'Filipino time' is tolerated socially and sometimes in meetings.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Korea arriving on time or a few minutes early for meetings and meals is expected and lateness reads as disrespect.
watch_outs.do: Plan to arrive five to ten minutes early for business meetings and family dinners.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not treat a business appointment with the relaxed lateness you might use for a social gathering at home.

watch_outs.title: Accept food offered by host
watch_outs.from_norm: In the Philippines you might decline outright when full, or accept a small token portion.
watch_outs.to_norm: In Korea refusing food a host offers can slight them; accepting at least a little is the gracious move.
watch_outs.do: Accept a small portion and eat some, even if you are full.
watch_outs.avoid: Do not push the plate away or say you are full before tasting what your host served.
